title: Tzav: the thanks offering (Leviticus 7:12)
hookLine: after a rescue, a thanks offering; midrash says thanks alone will never cease

lines: AT THE CHECKOUT, IN THE TAXI.
cards: Spend an hour in an Israeli supermarket, a taxi or a café, and today's word comes at you again and again. Todah.
It's how you say thank you in Hebrew: todah for the change, todah for the coffee, todah rabbah, thanks a lot. But before it was the word at the checkout counter, it was the name of an offering.
A very particular one, brought by a very particular kind of person: someone who had just been rescued.

teach.h: IF HE OFFER IT FOR A THANKSGIVING.
teach.b: Leviticus lists a family of offerings called peace offerings, and the first kind is this one: "If he offer it for a thanksgiving." Who brings it?

Rashi, drawing on the Talmud's reading of Psalm one hundred seven, names four kinds of people who come through danger: those who cross the sea, those who cross the desert, those who recover from serious illness, and those set free from prison.
Each has been rescued, and the todah is how they say so.

The offering came with a lot of bread, forty loaves by the rabbis' count, and the Torah says it all had to be eaten the same day and night. Some commentators point out the result: you couldn't eat forty loaves alone.
You had to invite people in, and over the meal you'd tell them what happened. The thanks became a party, and the party became a story.
Then a midrash in Leviticus Rabbah says that in the time to come, all the offerings will cease except the thanks offering, and all the prayers will cease except the prayer of thanks.
The idea seems to be that when everything is mended, no one will need to ask for anything or atone for anything, but people will still say thank you.
Today, with no Temple, the custom lives on in a blessing called ha-gomel, said in synagogue by someone who has come through danger, with the congregation answering.

how: A person who has come through danger, such as serious illness, a dangerous journey or release from captivity, recites the blessing ha-gomel at the Torah reading, and the congregation responds.

o: thanks: an offering after a rescue
peace: a greeting said at the door
a blessing: words said before a meal

games.q: what's inside the offering — tap the pairs.
p: eaten the same day, with guests

s: the thanks offering could be eaten slowly over a week
it had to be eaten the same day and night, so people were invited to share it.
a midrash says the thanks offering will never cease
in the time to come, all offerings cease except todah.
todah is only an ancient word, no longer used
it's how people say thank you in Hebrew today.

games.q: you've just recovered from a serious illness. you bring a thanks offering, with forty loaves, and it all has to be eaten by morning. what do you do?
o: eat what you can and throw out the rest.
invite friends and tell them what happened.
give the bread back to the priests.
games.why: commentators point out that you'd have to invite people in. the thanks becomes a meal, and the meal becomes the story of your rescue.

practice: Think of a time you came through something: a scary diagnosis that turned out fine, a near miss on the road, a hard year, a moment someone pulled you out.
Remember it clearly, without rushing: who helped, and what could have happened, and didn't? If you pray, say todah to God; if not, say it to the people who were there, even just in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Todah. Thanks. The offering brought after a rescue, and still the everyday Hebrew word for thank you.

orig.note: Hebrew: thanks, and the name of the thanks offering in Leviticus 7:12.

carryVoice: Your line: thanks outlasts everything. A rescue is worth a table full of guests. Day three hundred eighty-seven.
